Match the axes and align your panels to the direction of the comparison you actually want the reader to make

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Do students who sleep less get lower grades, and does it depend on their program?
text:
Do students who sleep less get lower grades, and does it depend on their program?

We have a survey of 1,000 students
Today we answer this question, and learn Chapter 12 (logical vectors) along the way

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text: Answer

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text: Answer: split by program

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: So how did we get here?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The plan for today
We rebuild the pipeline one action at a time.
Each action needs a different part of Chapter 12:








Step
Action
Chapter 12 tools we need




1
mutate()
comparisons (<, ==), if_else(), case_when()


2
filter()
missing values, is.na(), &, |, !, %in%


3
group_by() + summarize()
sum(), mean(), any(), all()










Not everything fits in this 80-minute lecture


I may leave some of the undiscussed functions or tools in an appendix table at the end of the slide deck. Each row will say what the tool does and which section of the chapter to read. You should definitely take a look at the text for more details.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Meet the data















About this data



This is a simulated survey for teaching this class. Don’t take the results seriously.
A blank cell means the student left the question unanswered. R reads it as NA
You will see those blanks cause trouble in a few minutes

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
What is a logical vector?







Definition


A logical vector is the simplest kind of vector: every element is exactly one of three values.

TRUE
FALSE
NA (missing)






Raw data rarely arrives as logical vectors
But you will create and use them in almost every analysis

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Where we are in the pipeline

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Modifying a column of data set
text:
Modifying a column of data set







mutate()


This function adds new columns or modifies existing ones in a data frame. It operates column-wise and preserves the total number of rows.




survey |>
  mutate(
    sleep_hours_week = sleep_hours * 7,
    high_sleep = sleep_hours > 7.5
  )







Checkpoint


What is the code from above trying to do?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Creating logical vectors
The comparison operators are:



Operator
Meaning




<
less than


<=
less than or equal to


>
greater than


>=
greater than or equal to


==
equal exactly to


!=
not equal to



Each one compares two values and returns TRUE or FALSE.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Who sleeps less than 6 hours?









short_sleep is a logical column
We can store it with mutate(), or use the same test directly inside filter()
What is .keep?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Choosing which columns survive
mutate() has a .keep argument that controls which columns appear in the result.







.keep =
Columns returned




"all" (default)
All original columns plus the new ones


"used"
Only the columns used to build the new ones, plus the new ones


"unused"
Original columns you did not use, plus the new ones


"none"
Only the new columns (plus any grouping variables)










Why we use it today


.keep = "used" shows each input column next to the logical column it produced, so you can check the result by eye. It does not change the logic.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: How many TRUE, FALSE, and NA?
text:
How many TRUE, FALSE, and NA?















A blank is not FALSE


Students who left sleep_hours blank get NA, not FALSE. R does not know whether they slept less than 6 hours.

We deal with these rows in later in Step 2 filter().

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Comparing text
has_early_class is stored as text ("Yes" / "No"). Comparisons work on text too:















Spelling and capitals matter


"Yes", "yes", and "YES" are three different values to R. Check how your data is spelled before you compare it. We will look at how we deal with text (strings) next class.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Assigning labels using Logicals







if_else(condition, true, false)


This function picks one value when the condition is TRUE and another when it is FALSE.













A blank sleep_hours stays NA
This works for two groups (TRUE vs FALSE conditions)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: What if we want three groups?
text:
What if we want three groups?







Piecewise functions


We could nest one if_else() inside another. Every extra group adds another layer.













It works, but it is already hard to read: time for case_when()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
case_when()

Inspired by SQL’s CASE statement
Uses a special syntax unlike anything else in the tidyverse: pairs of condition ~ output
condition must be a logical vector; when it is TRUE, output is used

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Check your groups









Where did the NA row come from?
No condition matched the blank sleep_hours, so case_when() gave NA

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Why “Normal” has no lower bound







Only the first match is used


If several conditions are TRUE for one student, case_when() uses the first one.





A student with sleep_hours = 5 is < 6 and <= 7.5
The "Short" line comes first, so it wins
That is why "Normal" does not need to say sleep_hours >= 6

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: What if we swap the order?
text:
What if we swap the order?















Overlapping conditions


There is no "Short" row any more. Every short sleeper matched <= 7.5 first. Be careful with complex case_when() statements, especially when you mix < and >.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: .default is a catch-all, and a trap
text:
.default is a catch-all, and a trap















Where did the NA row go?


.default also catches the blank rows. They are now labelled "Long", which is wrong. We wrote sleep_hours > 7.5 explicitly so blank rows stay NA.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Exercise 1







Live exercise


Use case_when() to create a grade_band column from avg_grade:

"Fail": below 50
"Pass": 50 to 69
"Good": 70 to 84
"Excellent": 85 and above

Then use count() to see how many students are in each band. What happens to students with a blank avg_grade?














survey |>
  mutate(
    grade_band = case_when(
      avg_grade < 50   ~ "Fail",
      avg_grade < 70   ~ "Pass",
      avg_grade < 85   ~ "Good",
      avg_grade >= 85  ~ "Excellent"
    )
  ) |>
  count(grade_band)

# The blank avg_grade rows show up as NA: no condition matched them.
survey |>
  mutate(
    grade_band = case_when(
      avg_grade < 50   ~ "Fail",
      avg_grade < 70   ~ "Pass",
      avg_grade < 85   ~ "Good",
      avg_grade >= 85  ~ "Excellent"
    )
  ) |>
  count(grade_band)

# The blank avg_grade rows show up as NA: no condition matched them.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Where we are in the pipeline

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
filter() keeps TRUE rows







Key idea


filter() keeps rows where the condition is TRUE. It drops rows where the condition is FALSE or NA.













Students with a blank sleep_hours are silently gone
Is that what we wanted?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Missing values are “contagious”

NA stands for the unknown
Almost any operation involving an unknown value gives an unknown result

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: The most confusing case: NA == NA
text:
The most confusing case: NA == NA








Easier to see with some context:

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Let’s find the blank rows
The obvious attempt:















Zero rows. Why?



sleep_hours == NA returns NA for every row
filter() drops rows where the condition is NA
So nothing is left

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The fix: is.na()







Key idea


Never test for missing values with == NA. Use is.na().












is.na(x) works on any type of vector. It returns TRUE for missing values and FALSE for everything else.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Keeping the complete rows
Put ! in front to flip TRUE and FALSE:









!is.na(x) reads as “x is not missing”
This is the first half of our pipeline’s filter() line

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Combining logical vectors
Once you have several logical vectors, combine them with Boolean algebra:



Operator
Meaning




&
and


|
or


!
not












In filter(), a comma means the same as &: filter(a, b) is filter(a & b)
That is why our pipeline has filter(!is.na(sleep_group), !is.na(avg_grade))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Venn diagrams

Common Boolean operations. x is the left circle, y is the right circle, and the shaded region shows what each operator selects. Figure from R for Data Science (2e), Fig. 12.1.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Missing values in Boolean algebra
The rules look inconsistent at first:

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Making sense of the NA rules
text:
Making sense of the NA rules
Remember: an NA in a logical vector means “could be TRUE or FALSE”.







Or (|): only one side needs to be TRUE



TRUE | TRUE and FALSE | TRUE are both TRUE
So NA | TRUE must be TRUE: whichever way the NA resolves, the result is TRUE
But NA | FALSE is NA: it depends on what the NA really is












And (&): both sides must be TRUE



NA & TRUE is NA: it depends on the NA
NA & FALSE is FALSE: at least one side is FALSE no matter what

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: R does not work like English
text:
R does not work like English







A tempting mistake


Suppose we want the high-stress students: stress level 4 or 5. In English that is easy to say…












It does not give an error, but it does not work either. Every row came back. Why?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
What went wrong?

R first evaluates stress_level == 4, producing a logical vector (call it four)
Then it computes four | 5
With a logical operator, any number other than 0 is converted to TRUE
So this becomes four | TRUE, which is always TRUE
Every row is selected

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The same mistake with text















Loud errors are the friendly ones


With numbers, the mistake is silent and gives wrong results. With text, R basically stops and complains. Either way, R does not read English the way we do, so you should write the full comparison on both sides.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The correct version








That gets long. There is a shortcut.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Is this in my vector?







x %in% y


This returns a logical vector the same length as x. It is TRUE whenever a value of x appears anywhere in y.












An easy way to dodge the == / | ordering problem:

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
%in% and missing values







Different NA rules


%in% follows different NA rules from ==: NA %in% NA is TRUE.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Back to the pipeline
By now we have removed the missing data under the columns with categorical variable with sleep_hours (i.e. sleep_group), and avg_grade.









Why do we also drop blank avg_grade? The next step averages it!

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Exercise 2







Live exercise



How many students left sleep_hours blank? Then count the blanks in every column.
Find students in Arts or Business who sleep less than 6 hours. Use %in%.
Find the same students again, this time using |.















# Part 1
survey |>
  summarize(n_missing = sum(is.na(sleep_hours)))

# Part 1b
survey |>
  summarize(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x))))

# Part 2
survey |>
  filter(program %in% c("Arts", "Business"), sleep_hours < 6)

# Part 3
survey |>
  filter(program == "Arts" | program == "Business", sleep_hours < 6)
# Part 1
survey |>
  summarize(n_missing = sum(is.na(sleep_hours)))

# Part 1b
survey |>
  summarize(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x))))

# Part 2
survey |>
  filter(program %in% c("Arts", "Business"), sleep_hours < 6)

# Part 3
survey |>
  filter(program == "Arts" | program == "Business", sleep_hours < 6)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Where we are in the pipeline

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Key Functions Here







group_by()


This function changes the unit of analysis by organizing rows into groups. It is invisible on its own, but changes how subsequent functions operate.











summarize()


This function collapses multiple rows down into a single summary statistic per group.




# Example: Calculate student counts and mean grades by program
survey |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean_grade = mean(avg_grade, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Summaries of logical vectors
In a numeric context, TRUE becomes 1 and FALSE becomes 0.







Key idea



sum(x) gives the number of TRUEs
mean(x) gives the proportion of TRUEs (because mean() is just sum() divided by length())

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
sum() and mean() by program
How many students in each program sleep under 6 hours, and what proportion is that?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Remember the NAs







Without na.rm


Try deleting na.rm = TRUE from the code above. One NA in a group makes the whole sum() or mean() NA.











na.rm changes the denominator


mean(x < 6, na.rm = TRUE) is the proportion among students who answered. It does not count blank rows as FALSE. In our pipeline, we avoid the problem by filtering the blank rows out first.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
any() and all()

any(x) is the equivalent of |: TRUE if there is at least one TRUE in x
all(x) is the equivalent of &: TRUE only if every value of x is TRUE
Like most summary functions, add na.rm = TRUE to drop missing values










Often any() and all() are a bit too crude
We usually want to know how many, which is why sum() and mean() come first

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Putting it together







Watch the group sizes


Look at the n column. Some groups have only 10 to 15 students, so their averages are less trustworthy than the large ones.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Back to the question

Do students who sleep less get lower grades, and does it depend on their program?


Overall: students who sleep more have higher average grades
Within each program:** the differences are small and not consistent
Why: programs differ in both sleep and grades, so mixing them together created the overall pattern








Caution: What we cannot say



This is survey data, so it shows association, not cause
Some groups are small, so differences of a point or two mean little
A good analyst checks the group sizes before telling a story

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Chapter summary
A logical vector is simple (each value is TRUE, FALSE, or NA), but it is very powerful.

Create them with >, <, <=, >=, ==, !=, and is.na()
Combine them with !, &, and |
Summarize them with any(), all(), sum(), and mean()
Transform conditionally with if_else() and case_when()

Why spreadsheets are tricky

People use spreadsheets for storage, sharing, and presentation all at once
So you get merged cells, notes above the data, mixed types, inconsistent headers

title: Getting Data into R
text:
The students spreadsheet: what’s wrong?
#>   `Student ID` `Full Name`   favourite.food   mealPlan   AGE
#>          <dbl> <chr>         <chr>            <chr>      <chr>
#> 3            3 Jayendra Lyne N/A              Breakfast… 7
#> 4            4 Leon Rossini  Anchovies        Lunch only <NA>
#> 5            5 Chidiegwu …   Pizza            Breakfast… five
Three problems to fix:

Messy column names
"N/A" isn’t recognized as a missing value
age is read as text (one entry is the word “five”)

title: Getting Data into R
section: Fixing it, one argument at a time
text:
Fixing it, one argument at a time
students <- read_excel(
  "data/students.xlsx",
  col_names = c("student_id", "full_name", "favourite_food",
                "meal_plan", "age"),       # 1. snake_case names
  skip = 1,                                # ...and drop the old header row
  na = c("", "N/A"),                       # 2. extra NA strings
  col_types = c("numeric", "text", "text", "text", "text")  # 3. keep age as text
)

students <- students |>
  mutate(
    age = if_else(age == "five", "5", age),
    age = parse_number(age)
  )

Forcing age to "numeric" would silently turn “five” into NA. Read as text, then clean in R.

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Worksheets
Spreadsheets can hold several worksheets.
excel_sheets("data/penguins.xlsx")
#> [1] "Torgersen Island" "Biscoe Island"    "Dream Island"

torgersen <- read_excel("data/penguins.xlsx",
                        sheet = "Torgersen Island", na = "NA")
biscoe    <- read_excel("data/penguins.xlsx",
                        sheet = "Biscoe Island", na = "NA")
dream     <- read_excel("data/penguins.xlsx",
                         sheet = "Dream Island", na = "NA")

penguins <- bind_rows(torgersen, biscoe, dream)
Chapter 26 shows how to avoid this repetition.

title: Getting Data into R

Reading part of a sheet
Real sheets often have notes above and below the data.
deaths_path <- readxl_example("deaths.xlsx")

read_excel(deaths_path, range = "A5:F15")

range uses spreadsheet notation: A5 is the top-left corner, F15 the bottom-right
Preferred over fiddling with skip and n_max

title: Getting Data into R
section: Data types: what you see isn’t what’s stored
text:
Data types: what you see isn’t what’s stored
An Excel cell is one of four things: boolean, number, datetime, or text.

Excel has no integers; everything is floating point, display formatting hides it
Dates are stored as numbers (days since 1 Jan 1900)
Something that looks numeric can actually be text

Recommended workflow:

Let readxl guess the types
Check the result
Re-import with col_types if needed ("list" handles mixed-type columns)

For exotic info like cell colour or bold text, look at tidyxl.

bake_sale <- tibble(

write_xlsx(bake_sale, path = "data/bake-sale.xlsx")

Column names are included and bolded by default
Type information is lost on a round trip (the factor comes back as text), so Excel is a poor format for caching interim results
Need styling or multiple sheets? Use openxlsx (not tidyverse-style: camelCase, no piping)

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Why databases?

Huge amounts of data live in them
Asking someone for a CSV snapshot every time doesn’t scale
You want to reach in and get the data when you need it

This chapter’s route:

DBI: connect and send SQL
dbplyr: write dplyr, get SQL
Use that translation to learn SQL

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Database basics
A database is a collection of tables (like data frames), but:

Tables live on disk and can be arbitrarily large
Tables almost always have indexes for fast lookup
Classic databases are row-oriented (built for collecting data); newer column-oriented ones are faster for analysis

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Three kinds of DBMS


Client-server
Central server, you connect as a client.
PostgreSQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle

Cloud
Like client-server but hosted; scales on demand.
Snowflake, Redshift, BigQuery

In-process
Runs entirely on your computer.
SQLite, duckdb

The book uses duckdb: no server setup, and fast.

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Connecting with DBI
library(DBI)
library(dbplyr)

con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
Other DBMSs differ only in the connection call:
con <- DBI::dbConnect(
  RPostgres::Postgres(),
  hostname = "databases.mycompany.com",
  port = 1234
)

Always use DBI, plus a DBMS-specific package (RPostgres, RMariaDB…)
No dedicated package? Try odbc
Ask your team or DBA for connection details

title: Getting Data into R
section: Putting data in and checking it
text:
Putting data in and checking it
dbWriteTable(con, "mpg", ggplot2::mpg)
dbWriteTable(con, "diamonds", ggplot2::diamonds)

dbListTables(con)
#> [1] "diamonds" "mpg"

con |> dbReadTable("diamonds") |> as_tibble()
Already know SQL? Send it directly:
sql <- "
  SELECT carat, cut, clarity, color, price
  FROM diamonds
  WHERE price > 15000
"
as_tibble(dbGetQuery(con, sql))

title: Getting Data into R
section: dbplyr: dplyr with a different backend
text:
dbplyr: dplyr with a different backend
tbl() creates an object that represents a table:
diamonds_db <- tbl(con, "diamonds")
The object is lazy: dplyr verbs just record what you want and nothing runs until needed.
big_diamonds_db <- diamonds_db |>
  filter(price > 15000) |>
  select(carat:clarity, price)
Row count shows as ?? because counting would require running the whole query.

title: Getting Data into R
text:
See the SQL, then collect
big_diamonds_db |> show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT carat, cut, color, clarity, price
#> FROM diamonds
#> WHERE (price > 15000.0)

big_diamonds <- big_diamonds_db |> collect()

show_query(): a great way to learn SQL from dplyr you already know
collect(): run the query and pull results into an in-memory tibble


Typical pattern: filter and aggregate in the database, then collect() and finish in R.

title: Getting Data into R
text:
SQL basics

Top-level pieces are statements (CREATE, INSERT, SELECT); we focus on SELECT queries
A query is made of clauses: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, ORDER BY
SELECT and FROM are always required: SELECT * FROM table

Two key differences from dplyr:

Case doesn’t matter (convention: keywords in UPPERCASE)
Order matters: write SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, ORDER BY


Written order ≠ evaluation order. SQL evaluates FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → SELECT → ORDER BY.

title: Getting Data into R
text:
dplyr verb → SQL clause



dplyr
SQL




select(), rename(), relocate(), mutate()
SELECT


summarize()
SELECT (with GROUP BY)


group_by()
GROUP BY


filter()
WHERE (or HAVING after a summary)


arrange()
ORDER BY


*_join()
JOIN … ON inside FROM

title: Getting Data into R
section: SELECT, GROUP BY, WHERE, ORDER BY in action

title: Getting Data into R
text:
SQL quirks to remember

Renaming is aliasing with AS; the old name goes on the left
= for comparison (not ==); AND/OR instead of &/|; IN instead of %in%
Strings use single quotes; double quotes mark column/table names
NULL instead of NA: silently dropped in aggregations
Filtering on a summarized value becomes HAVING, because WHERE runs before aggregation

diamonds_db |> group_by(cut) |> summarize(n = n()) |> filter(n > 100)
#> ... GROUP BY cut
#> HAVING (COUNT(*) > 100.0)

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Subqueries and joins
Subqueries: needed when a SELECT can’t reference a column it just created.
flights |> mutate(year1 = year + 1, year2 = year1 + 1) |> show_query()
#> SELECT *, year1 + 1.0 AS year2
#> FROM (
#>   SELECT *, "year" + 1.0 AS year1
#>   FROM flights
#> ) AS q01
Joins use ON inside FROM:
flights |> left_join(planes |> rename(year_built = year), join_by(tailnum))
#> FROM flights
#> LEFT JOIN planes
#>   ON (flights.tailnum = planes.tailnum)
Many tables to connect? The dm package can map the keys for you.

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Translating R functions

Simple summaries translate directly (mean() → AVG()); more statistical ones are more complex (median())
Inside mutate(), summaries become window functions with OVER (PARTITION BY …)
lead() / lag() also become window functions, so arrange() first (tables have no intrinsic order)
if_else(), case_when(), and cut() all become CASE WHEN

flights |> mutate(description = if_else(arr_delay > 0, "delayed", "on-time"))
#> SELECT CASE WHEN (arr_delay > 0.0) THEN 'delayed'
#>             WHEN NOT (arr_delay > 0.0) THEN 'on-time' END AS description
Not every R function is translated yet; see vignette("translation-function", package = "dbplyr").

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Chapter 21 takeaways

DBI connects and runs SQL; dbplyr translates dplyr to SQL
Queries are lazy: show_query() to inspect, collect() to run
Knowing some SQL is valuable: it’s the common language for data work
Next steps: SQL for Data Scientists (Teate), Practical SQL (DeBarros)

title: Getting Data into R
text:
The problem with CSV

CSV is simple, human-readable, and universal
But it’s inefficient: lots of work to read into R
Alternative: Parquet, an open binary format, paired with Apache Arrow

library(tidyverse)
library(arrow)
The arrow package is a dplyr backend for larger-than-memory datasets.

title: Getting Data into R
text:
arrow or dbplyr?
Often the choice is made for you: the data is already in a database or in parquet files.
If you’re starting from your own CSVs, you can either:

load them into a database, or
convert them to parquet

Early on, try both and see which works better for you.

title: Getting Data into R
text:
The example: Seattle library checkouts

~41 million rows: monthly checkouts per title, April 2005 – October 2022
A 9 GB CSV file, too big to comfortably load with read_csv()
Rule of thumb: you want at least twice the data size in RAM

curl::multi_download(
  "https://r4ds.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/seattle-library-checkouts.csv",
  "data/seattle-library-checkouts.csv",
  resume = TRUE
)
curl::multi_download() gives a progress bar and can resume interrupted downloads.

title: Getting Data into R
Getting Data into R
text:
Why parquet?

Smaller: efficient encodings and compression
Rich types: column types are stored with the data (no guessing dates vs strings)
Column-oriented: matches how analysis reads data
Chunked: parts can be processed in parallel, and some can be skipped


Downside: not human-readable. Far fewer tools read parquet than CSV.

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Partitioning
Split a large dataset across many files.

Partition by variables you filter on, so arrow can skip files
Rough guide: avoid files under 20 MB or over 2 GB, and avoid more than 10,000 files
No hard rules, so experiment

pq_path <- "data/seattle-library-checkouts"

seattle_csv |>
  group_by(CheckoutYear) |>
  write_dataset(path = pq_path, format = "parquet")

title: Getting Data into R
text:
What we get

One 9 GB CSV → 18 parquet files, roughly 100–300 MB each
Total about 4 GB, a little over half the CSV size
Hive-style folder names: CheckoutYear=2005/part-0.parquet

seattle_pq <- open_dataset(pq_path)

title: Getting Data into R
Getting Data into R
text:
Performance: CSV vs parquet
Books checked out per month in 2021:



Format
Elapsed time




Single CSV
~11 seconds


Partitioned parquet
~0.06 seconds



~100× faster, for two reasons:

Partitioning: only 1 of the 18 files is read
Columnar format: only the 4 columns used are read

title: Getting Data into R
Getting Data into R
text:
Chapter 22 takeaways

open_dataset() works with CSV or parquet without loading everything
Convert big CSVs to partitioned parquet with write_dataset()
Use familiar dplyr verbs; collect() runs the query
to_duckdb() bridges arrow and databases

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Rectangling
Rectangling = turning tree-like data into a data frame of rows and columns.
Hierarchical data is common, especially from the web. The plan:

Understand lists
Learn two tidyr functions: unnest_longer() and unnest_wider()
Work through case studies
Understand JSON

library(tidyverse)
library(repurrrsive)
library(jsonlite)

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Lists
Lists can hold elements of different types, including other lists.
x1 <- list(1:4, "a", TRUE)
x2 <- list(a = 1:2, b = 1:3, c = 1:4)   # named children

str(x2)
#> List of 3
#>  $ a: int [1:2] 1 2
#>  $ b: int [1:3] 1 2 3
#>  $ c: int [1:4] 1 2 3 4

str() gives a compact view of structure
For big lists, switch to View() in RStudio (it even shows the subsetting code)

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Nested lists vs c()
x3 <- list(list(1, 2), list(3, 4))   # a list of lists: hierarchy
x4 <- c(list(1, 2), list(3, 4))      # c() flattens to a list of 4
x5 <- list(1, list(2, list(3, list(4, list(5)))))
str(x5)
#> List of 2
#>  $ : num 1
#>  $ :List of 2
#>   ..$ : num 2
#>   ..$ :List of 2
#>   .. ..$ : num 3
#> ...

title: Getting Data into R
text:
List-columns
Lists can live inside a tibble.
df <- tibble(
  x = 1:2,
  y = c("a", "b"),
  z = list(list(1, 2), list(3, 4, 5))
)
#>       x y     z
#>   <int> <chr> <list>
#> 1     1 a     <list [2]>
#> 2     2 b     <list [3]>

They behave like any other column (you can filter() on x)
Computing on them is hard, so we’ll unnest them into regular variables
Easier with tibble() than data.frame()

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Two flavours of list-column


Named children
Same names in every row.
→ become columns
unnest_wider()

Unnamed children
Number of elements varies per row.
→ become rows
unnest_longer()

title: Getting Data into R
text:
unnest_wider()
df1 <- tribble(
  ~x, ~y,
  1, list(a = 11, b = 12),
  2, list(a = 21, b = 22),
  3, list(a = 31, b = 32),
)

df1 |> unnest_wider(y)
#>       x     a     b
#> 1     1    11    12
#> 2     2    21    22
#> 3     3    31    32

df1 |> unnest_wider(y, names_sep = "_")   # columns: x, y_a, y_b
names_sep prevents name clashes.

title: Getting Data into R
text:
unnest_longer()
df2 <- tribble(
  ~x, ~y,
  1, list(11, 12, 13),
  2, list(21),
  3, list(31, 32),
)

df2 |> unnest_longer(y)
#>       x     y
#> 1     1    11
#> 2     1    12
#> 3     1    13
#> 4     2    21
#> 5     3    31
#> 6     3    32

x is repeated for each element
Empty list → the row disappears (use keep_empty = TRUE to keep it as NA)

title: Getting Data into R
Getting Data into R
section: Other tidyr functions to know about
text:
Other tidyr functions to know about

unnest_auto(): picks wider or longer for you. Fine for exploration, but it hides your data’s structure
unnest(): expands rows and columns; useful for list-columns containing data frames (common in tidymodels)

title: Getting Data into R
Getting Data into R
Getting Data into R
text:
Case study 3: deeply nested (gmaps_cities)
Google geocoding results for five cities. Alternate the two functions:
locations <- gmaps_cities |>
  unnest_wider(json) |>        # results + status
  select(-status) |>
  unnest_longer(results) |>    # one row per match
  unnest_wider(results)        # address, geometry, ...
Washington and Arlington each get two matches (state/DC, Texas/Virginia).

title: Getting Data into R
Getting Data into R
text:
JSON data types
JSON is how most web APIs return data. Six types:



JSON
R equivalent




null
NA


string (double quotes only)
character


number (no Inf/NaN)
numeric


true / false
TRUE / FALSE


array [1, 2, 3]
unnamed list


object {"x": 1}
named list



No native dates (stored as strings → parse_date()); sometimes numbers arrive as strings (→ parse_double()).

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Reading JSON with jsonlite
library(jsonlite)

gh_users2 <- read_json(gh_users_json())      # from a file

str(parse_json('{"x": [1, 2, 3]}'))          # from a string
#> List of 1
#>  $ x:List of 3
#>   ..$ : int 1
#>   ..$ : int 2
#>   ..$ : int 3
The book avoids fromJSON() because its automatic simplification hides what’s happening. Rectangle it yourself.

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Starting the rectangling process
Top-level array (most common): one row per element.
json <- '[{"name": "John", "age": 34}, {"name": "Susan", "age": 27}]'
tibble(json = parse_json(json)) |> unnest_wider(json)
Top-level object: wrap it in a list first.
df <- tibble(json = list(parse_json(json)))
df |>
  unnest_wider(json) |>
  unnest_longer(results) |>
  unnest_wider(results)
Or reach in and start from the part you want: tibble(results = parse_json(json)$results).

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Chapter 23 takeaways

Hierarchical data = lists; in tibbles, list-columns
Only two core tools: unnest_longer() (→ rows) and unnest_wider() (→ columns)
Repeat them as many times as the nesting requires; hoist() shortcuts known paths
JSON maps closely onto R lists (arrays ↔︎ unnamed, objects ↔︎ named)

title: Getting Data into R
text:
When there’s no API

If a site offers an API, prefer it: more reliable (JSON → Chapter 23)
If not, you can still scrape the HTML with rvest

library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Ethics and legality
Not legal advice. Consult a lawyer when in doubt.
Rule of thumb: you’re likely fine if the data is public, non-personal, and factual.

Be respectful: pause between requests; the polite package does this and caches pages
Terms of service: often forbid scraping; respect where possible. Binding-ness depends on jurisdiction and on whether you took an explicit action (account, checkbox)
Personally identifiable information: be extremely careful (GDPR; the OkCupid study is a cautionary tale)
Copyright: facts aren’t protected, original content may be (fair use might apply)

title: Getting Data into R
Getting Data into R
Getting Data into R
text:
CSS selectors: the essential three



Selector
Matches




p
all <p> elements


.title
elements with class="title"


#title
the element with id="title" (unique)



html |> html_elements("p")           # both paragraphs
html |> html_elements(".important")   # one
html |> html_elements("#first")       # one

title: Getting Data into R
text:
html_element() vs html_elements()

html_elements() → all matches (zero matches → empty result)
html_element() → one result per input (no match → NA)


Combine them: html_elements() to find observations, then html_element() to find variables.
characters <- html |> html_elements("li")     # one per character

characters |> html_element(".weight")         # 4 results, NA for missing
characters |> html_elements(".weight")        # only 3, connection to names lost!

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Extracting text and attributes
characters |> html_element("b") |> html_text2()
#> [1] "C-3PO"  "R4-P17" "R2-D2"  "Yoda"

characters |> html_element(".weight") |> html_text2()
#> [1] "167 kg" NA       "96 kg"  "66 kg"

html |>
  html_elements("p") |>
  html_element("a") |>
  html_attr("href")

Use html_text2(), not html_text(): better handling of nested HTML
html_attr() always returns strings; convert numbers/dates yourself

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Tables
HTML tables (<table>, <tr>, <th>, <td>) have a shortcut:
html |>
  html_element(".mytable") |>
  html_table()
#>       x     y
#> 1   1.5   2.7
#> 2   4.9   1.3
#> 3   7.2   8.1

Numbers are converted automatically
Turn that off with convert = FALSE if it misbehaves

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Finding the right selector
The hardest part: you want selectors that are both specific (no extras) and sensitive (catch everything).

SelectorGadget: click positive/negative examples to generate a selector
Browser dev tools (Chrome: right-click → Inspect): explore the HTML; Copy as Selector
Selectors Explained translates selectors into plain English
Learn more with the CSS Dinner game and MDN docs

Lots of trial and error is normal.

title: Getting Data into R
Getting Data into R
text:
Case study: IMDb top 250
Start with html_table(), then tidy:
table <- html |> html_element("table") |> html_table()

ratings <- table |>
  select(rank_title_year = `Rank & Title`, rating = `IMDb Rating`) |>
  mutate(rank_title_year = str_replace_all(rank_title_year, "\n +", " ")) |>
  separate_wider_regex(
    rank_title_year,
    patterns = c(rank = "\\d+", "\\. ", title = ".+", " +\\(",
                 year = "\\d+", "\\)")
  )
Look at the raw HTML too: a title attribute held the number of votes, which the table didn’t show.
html |> html_elements("td strong") |> html_attr("title")
#> "9.2 based on 2,536,415 user ratings"

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Dynamic sites

rvest downloads raw HTML and doesn’t run JavaScript
If the page builds its content with JavaScript, html_elements() may return nothing like what you see in the browser
Workaround: simulate a full browser (via the chromote package); check the rvest site for current status








Warning


Scraping code is fragile: if the site changes its structure, your code breaks.

title: Getting Data into R
text:
Chapter 24 takeaways

Check ethics and legality first: public, non-personal, factual; be polite
HTML → elements and attributes; CSS selectors pick them out
html_elements() for observations, html_element() for variables, then html_text2() / html_attr() / html_table()
Expect trial and error, and expect breakage when sites change

title: Getting Data into R
text:
The whole import toolkit







Where the data lives
Reach for




Excel / Google Sheets
read_excel(), read_sheet()


A database
DBI + dbplyr (tbl(), show_query(), collect())


Huge files on disk
